Directions [Set of 4 Questions]: Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

In China, there once lived a father, his four sons, and three daughters-in-law. His three older sons had married within a few months of each other and all with young women from the same village. Recently, these three new daughters-in-law had been brought into the house. Their new father-in-law's wife had died a few years before and having no mother-in-law with them in their new home, and being lonesome and homesick for their former families, they constantly asked the old man for permission to visit their former village. For you see, those were the days when young women, after they married and moved into the homes of their new husbands, needed permission to leave the household. Annoyed by the continual pleas of his three new daughters-in-law, the old father thought of a way to put an end to it.

He gave the young women permission in this way, saying, "You are always begging me to allow you to go and visit your mothers, and you think I am very hard-hearted for not letting you go. Now you may go, but only upon this condition. When you come back, you must each bring me something that I want. One of you must bring me some fire in paper, the other must bring me some wind in paper, and the third must bring me some music in wind. Unless you promise to bring me this, you are never to ask me to let you go home. And if you go and fail to get these for me, you are never to come back." The old man did not suppose that these conditions would be accepted. Of course, they were hard to understand, much less to fulfil. But the girls were young and thoughtless, and in their anxiety to get away did not consider any of that. So, they promised and made ready with speed. In great glee, they started off on foot to visit their mothers.

Which of the following questions cannot be answered on the basis of the above passage?
options_en: How many sons did the old man have?
Which son did not get married?
Where did the old man's daughters-in-law want to go?
Why did one of his sons not marry?
questions.solution_en:
The answer of option (a) is four (as given in the first paragraph of the passage).

The answer of option (b) is - the youngest one, as it's mentioned in the first paragraph of the passage that the three older sons were married.

The answer of option (c) is - their former village (as given in the first paragraph of the passage).

There's nowhere mentioned the reason why the youngest son wasn't married. Hence, (d) is the correct answer.

Directions [Set of 4 Questions]:Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

Jenna had just moved into a new apartment in the heart of the city. She had spent the entire day unpacking and arranging her stuff in her new home. She was exhausted, so she decided to take a break and explore the neighbourhood. She wandered down the bustling streets, taking in the sights and sounds of the city. As she was walking, she noticed an antique shop tucked away in a quiet alley. Curiosity got the best of her, and she decided to go in and take a look around. The shop was filled with all sorts of unique items, but one caught Jenna's eye - an ornate key with intricate designs etched into it. Jenna knew she had to have it. She purchased the key and brought it back to her apartment. She tried it in every lock in her new home, but none of them seemed to fit. Frustrated, she put the key down and went to bed. The next morning, Jenna woke up to find that the key was missing. She searched high and low, but it was nowhere to be found. She retraced her steps from the previous day, but no one had seen it. Days turned into weeks, and Jenna was starting to lose hope of ever finding the key again. That is until she received a package in the mail. Inside was a note that read, "I found your key. Meet me at the antique shop where you purchased it." Jenna rushed to the antique shop, and there she found an elderly man waiting for her. He handed her the key and explained that it had been passed down through generations of his family. He wanted her to have it, as he believed she was meant to find it. Jenna was overwhelmed with gratitude and felt a sense of belonging in her new home. The key may have been lost for a time, but it ultimately led her to a meaningful connection with the past.

What does the word "belonging" mean in the context of the passage?
options_en: Feeling at home in a place
Owning something
Having a sense of superiority
Losing something
questions.solution_en:
The passage mentions that Jenna felt a sense of belonging in her new home after receiving the key and connecting with the past. So, option (a) will be the appropriate choice here.

Hence, option (a) is correct.

questions.q_en:
Directions [Set of 4 Questions]: Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

I sat motionless in the passenger seat, feeling trapped in my tight seat belt while Mom sang along with her tapes and pointed at everything she spotted on the roadside. "Oh, Mary, please don't be moody, not today. I told Harry all about how polite and intelligent and cheerful you are," she said. Harry was my mother's new boyfriend, her "significant other," she called him. She'd met him at a business meeting when her company bought the company Harry worked for, and since then she'd been driving over the border to Canada every weekend to see him, leaving me at Dad's. Don't get me wrong, I loved staying with Dad, but I missed my Mom-weekends. We used to make popcorn and watch late-night TV, then sleep in and eat cold breakfast cereal together. Now, when she came to pick me up on Sunday afternoons, she always looked glowing and energetic - and much happier than she ever looked after a weekend spent with me. Last Monday she said something about her and Harry getting married, and that this trip might be the time when he pops the question. The only obstacle before him was meeting me. "I'll be sugar and spice and everything nice, I promise," I said sarcastically, staring out at the Canadian countryside. It pretty much resembled the American countryside only . . . it was more Canadian, somehow. Bigger and emptier, just as I imagined Harry; bigger than Dad, with an enormous head with lots of empty space inside.

According to the passage, which of the following is the correct synonym of the word 'pick up' in the passage?
options_en: begin
pull
lift
fetch
questions.solution_en:
The given passage states that "Now, when she came to pick me up on Sunday afternoons...". In the given sentence, the phrasal verb 'pick up' means 'go somewhere to collect someone, typically in one's car.'

Begin: perform or undergo the first part of (an action or activity).

Pull: exert force on (someone or something) so as to cause movement towards oneself.

Lift: raise to a higher position or level.

Fetch: go for and then bring back (someone or something) for someone.

Among the given options, 'fetch' is the most appropriate synonym of the given phrasal verb.

Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

Note:

Phrasal verb: A phrase that consists of a verb with a preposition or adverb or both, the meaning of which is different from the meaning of its separate parts. Example: She has always looked down on me. Here, the phrasal verb 'to look down on someone' doesn't mean that you are looking down from a higher place at someone who is below you; it means that you think that you are better than someone.

Directions [Set of 4 Questions]: Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

I sat motionless in the passenger seat, feeling trapped in my tight seat belt while Mom sang along with her tapes and pointed at everything she spotted on the roadside. "Oh, Mary, please don't be moody, not today. I told Harry all about how polite and intelligent and cheerful you are," she said. Harry was my mother's new boyfriend, her "significant other," she called him. She'd met him at a business meeting when her company bought the company Harry worked for, and since then she'd been driving over the border to Canada every weekend to see him, leaving me at Dad's. Don't get me wrong, I loved staying with Dad, but I missed my Mom-weekends. We used to make popcorn and watch late-night TV, then sleep in and eat cold breakfast cereal together. Now, when she came to pick me up on Sunday afternoons, she always looked glowing and energetic - and much happier than she ever looked after a weekend spent with me. Last Monday she said something about her and Harry getting married, and that this trip might be the time when he pops the question. The only obstacle before him was meeting me. "I'll be sugar and spice and everything nice, I promise," I said sarcastically, staring out at the Canadian countryside. It pretty much resembled the American countryside only . . . it was more Canadian, somehow. Bigger and emptier, just as I imagined Harry; bigger than Dad, with an enormous head with lots of empty space inside.

Why did Mary's mother find that trip special?
options_en: Harry was going to introduce her to his family.
She was going to be married that weekend.
She was going to meet Harry after a long time.
She thought Harry was going to propose to her.

questions.q_en:
Directions [Set of 4 Questions]: Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

With cracked plaster and peeling paint, I considered what I could say. Water damage would've been the easy answer, but I opted for the truth: "My phone rang." As expected, these words settled somewhere beyond her reach, so she gave my comment its only sensible response: "Maybe you should turn down the ringer." "Come here, let me explain why I hate phones, and why my father is to blame. He was a troubled man," I said, because that's how it had been said to me. She listened with attentive eyes, but I knew she'd be confused by what I said next: "And he'd play Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera. Over and over." She lowered her head in search of a link and looked up when she found one. "Is that solitaire?" This time I allowed a smile. "Sometimes he'd conduct an invisible orchestra, waving arms in an erratic fashion, and sometimes he'd sit and listen. But Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera, that one commanded a different reaction. From the start, he stood at full attention, motionless until the end. It went like this for a long time, then he left."

"I soon became his replacement. I'd sit in the study and listen to his music. One evening mother said he wanted to talk to me. I asked if I was going to see him and she said that he'd call. I asked if I could use the phone in his study and she said I could." At this point my companion, attentive as ever, offered her second assumption of the evening, and though more likely than the first, it was just as wrong: "And he never called and that's why you hate phones." No, that's not why. "When mother told me he was on the line, I rushed to the study and dropped the needle on Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera, then picked up the phone. He didn't say hello or ask how I was, he only said that there's no peace in the world. He'd looked, it wasn't there, not for him." With her final assumption, she came closer to the truth: "So phones remind you of your father, and that's why you hate them."

"That's part of it," I said, "but there's more. He said he could hear Vivaldi in the background and told me to keep listening, that aria was on to something. Then he said goodbye to me and mother and everyone else. Forever. He found his peace." The music prevented a silence that would've felt more comfortable, then it finally stopped and I let the silence prevail. And there we sat, speaking without speaking, until the silence was shattered by a ring. I stood and walked to the phone, picked it up, not just the receiver, but all of it, and paused to admire the artistry.

What caused the speaker to sabotage his/her phone?
options_en: The speaker didn't like the ringtone.
Because their father didn't call, the speaker ruined the phone.
The speaker had found comfort in silence since their father's departure.
The behaviour of the speaker's father made them hate music.
questions.solution_en: The last paragraph of the passage states that the speaker found console in silence and escaped the memories of her father. So, option (c) is the correct choice.
questions.solution_hi: The last paragraph of the passage states that the speaker found console in silence and escaped the memories of her father. So, option (c) is the correct choice.

Directions [Set of 4 Questions]: Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

Once upon a time, in a grand estate perched on a hill, there lived an arrogant woman named Victoria. Victoria had recently married a wealthy widower, becoming the stepmother to his young son, Thomas. Her arrival brought an air of entitlement and superiority that cast a shadow over their once happy home. Victoria saw Thomas as an obstacle to her new life of luxury. She resented his presence, considering him an inconvenience that stood in the way of her ambitions. Thomas, despite his tender age, possessed a resilient spirit. He yearned for his father's love and acceptance, but Victoria's coldness only incited his determination to rise above her contemptuous behaviour. He sought solace in his own imagination, finding refuge in books and daydreams that transported him far away from the reality of their toxic household.

Victoria's arrogance began to crumble as she witnessed the positive impact Thomas had on others. She saw his unwavering kindness and the light he brought into their home. Slowly, her heart softened, and she realized the error of her ways. Regret filled her as she reflected on the years of mistreatment and the missed opportunities to build a genuine bond with Thomas. In a moment of vulnerability, Victoria approached Thomas, seeking forgiveness for her past actions. With tears in her eyes, she expressed her remorse and acknowledged the hurt she had caused. Thomas, in a display of grace beyond his years, embraced her with forgiveness, understanding that everyone deserves a chance to change.

From that day forward, Victoria and Thomas worked to rebuild their relationship. Their story became a testament to the transformative power of humility and forgiveness. Victoria learned that true strength lies not in arrogance, but in the ability to acknowledge one's mistakes and grow from them. And Thomas, through his resilience and capacity for forgiveness, showed that love can prevail, even in the face of adversity. In the end, their journey together taught them both valuable lessons about the importance of compassion, empathy, and the capacity for change.

What kind of passage is it?
options_en: Expository
Persuasive
Narrative
Reflective
questions.solution_en:
Expository Passage: This passage provides information or explains a concept or idea. It presents facts, evidence, or arguments in a logical and organized manner to educate or inform the reader.

Persuasive Passage: This passage aims to convince or persuade the reader to adopt a particular viewpoint or take a specific action. It often utilizes rhetorical devices, emotional appeals, and logical reasoning to make a persuasive argument.

Narrative Passage: This passage tells a story or recounts a sequence of events. It typically includes characters, and a plot, and may have a specific narrative structure, such as an introduction, rising action, climax, and resolution.

Reflective Passage: This passage involves introspection or personal reflection on experiences, thoughts, or emotions. It delves into the writer's inner thoughts and feelings, often offering insights or lessons learned.

This passage incorporates elements of character development, conflict, and a moral lesson, which are all typical of a fictional narrative.

Hence, option (c) is correct.
